items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists trick cancer cells into making the drugs that kill them
items.content_html: Scientists have developed a promising new cancer-fighting strategy that uses carbon monoxide naturally produced by tumor cells to manufacture powerful drugs inside the cancer cells themselves. Early laboratory experiments suggest the technique could selectively attack cancer while sparing healthy cells, potentially paving the way for safer chemotherapy alternatives.

items.title: [Nautilus] Could One Brain Region Be Tied to Feeling Sick All Over?
items.content_html:
When you break your foot, the pain is mostly confined to your foot. When you get the flu or another systemic infection, your entire being aches: Lethargy creeps into your limbs, your appetite vanishes, your temperature jags between scorching and chilled to the bone, and you just want to pull the covers over your head.

This kind of overpowering mind-body malaise is known as “sickness syndrome,” and it’s considered a distinct physiological and emotional state. Scientists believe sickness syndrome helps the body prepare to fight infections, but they don’t fully understand what is happening in the brain when this storm cloud descends.

Read more: “How to Unlearn a Disease”

The post Could One Brain Region Be Tied to Feeling Sick All Over? appeared first on Nautilus.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] The brain’s hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD
items.content_html: A surprising new discovery suggests that fear may cause the brain to blur the line between danger and safety rather than distinguish them more clearly. By observing brain activity in mice using augmented reality, scientists found that memories of threatening and harmless environments began to overlap, potentially allowing faster responses to danger. This "better safe than sorry" survival mechanism could help explain why people with anxiety or PTSD sometimes experience intense fear in completely safe situations.

items.title: [The Guardian Global Development] The Amazon’s canary in the coalmine: what a tropical fish can tell us about climate upheaval
items.content_html:
Scientist Adalberto Luis Val’s pioneering research on the tambaqui fish is revealing the effect of climate disruption in Brazil, with global implications for biodiversity and food security

As a boy in rural São Paulo, Adalberto Luis Val used to stare into the lake where his father took him fishing and wonder how all those creatures swimming below stayed alive. One day, he netted a few, put them in a jar, and brought them home to observe. The next morning, they were all dead. Val was devastated but intrigued.

“I needed to know how fish are able to live,” he says.

items.content_html: Researchers here report on the results of screening a few thousand proteins found in blood plasma for those where levels correlate with (a) risk of mortality and (b) organ-specific biological age, using a consensus approach to determining those biological age measures from proteomic data. The usual caveats apply regarding whether or not such an aging clock is actually measuring biological age, or would still produce decent data if an anti-aging intervention were involved, but gathering more data on the performance of such clocks is nonetheless a potentially useful activity. items.title: [ScienceDaily] All 5 genetic “letters” of DNA and RNA discovered in a 4.5-billion-year-old asteroid
items.content_html: Scientists have discovered all five essential nucleobases used in DNA and RNA in pristine samples from asteroid Ryugu, revealing that key ingredients for life existed in space billions of years ago. The remarkable finding adds to growing evidence from other asteroids and meteorites that these molecules were widespread throughout the early Solar System.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists reverse liver cell aging and cut Alzheimer’s-linked protein in half
items.content_html: A surprising discovery suggests that rejuvenating the liver could help protect against Alzheimer’s disease and heart disease. USC researchers found that an experimental drug restored aging liver cells in rats, cutting levels of an Alzheimer’s-linked protein in half and bringing bad cholesterol down to youthful levels. The treatment also revived a previously unknown communication system that helps liver cells remove harmful substances from the bloodstream.

items.content_html: Mysterious particles called neutrinos constantly stream through our bodies, and scientists are now detecting incredibly powerful versions arriving from distant cosmic sources using a massive observatory buried in Antarctic ice. These elusive “ghost particles” could hold extraordinary clues about the Big Bang, extreme cosmic events, and some of the universe’s greatest mysteries.

items.title: [New Atlas] Harvard smartphone app guides the blind faster, with fewer collisions
items.content_html:
If you have standard human vision (even if assisted by glasses), chances are you’re adept at finding things, people, and paths to them. Fortunately, plenty of new high-tech tools offer assistance, including robot guide dogs, a cane-bot (looking a bit like a small R2D2 with giant wheels), multiple types of smart glasses with descriptive audio, and even a haptic vest for blind dogs.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists discover a bacterial defense so strange they thought it was broken
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Scientists have discovered a bizarre bacterial defense system that works almost completely backward from anything seen before. Unlike typical bacterial immune systems that keep a deadly toxin under control until a virus attacks, this unusual mechanism waits until an infection begins before producing the DNA that switches on its lethal weapon. The infected bacterium then destroys itself, preventing the virus from multiplying and spreading to neighboring cells.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] Hackers hijacked a Claude Code extension, exposing yet another new AI security risk
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

The world can feel particularly unsafe these days, with AI agents running rampant within private networks and billions of dollars disappearing from crypto wallets in less time than it takes to watch a sitcom episode.

But while the world was watching Binance’s massive crypto heist, another potentially consequential security breach was unfolding largely under the radar.

For roughly 11 hours, a malicious version of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension was available on Cursor’s VS Code extension marketplace. The extension—which allows developers to use Anthropic’s AI coding assistant within Cursor to write, edit, and debug software—had been tampered with to collect information about users’ computers and attempt to install a persistent backdoor. That backdoor used Secure Shell (SSH), a tool for remotely accessing computers, and could potentially have allowed hackers to access victims’ machines even after the extension was removed.

Cursor disclosed the breach in a blog post, saying it removed the compromised extension as soon as it discovered the problem. The company also emphasized that the mechanism intended to give hackers remote access was unlikely to have worked in many cases because of flaws in its code. Anthropic, meanwhile, said in a statement that the incident “only impacts Cursor users” and was unrelated to Anthropic’s own systems.

According to Cursor’s security notice, the malicious extension was designed to leave behind scripts that would attempt to reconnect to the hackers’ server every minute, even after the extension had been removed. Cursor says it has since worked with the server’s hosting provider to take the server offline and to temporarily shut down and rebuild its extension marketplace. The company found no evidence that other extensions were compromised. Still, it is urging anyone who installed the affected version on October 29 to check their computers for signs of infection, remove any unauthorized access, and consider changing potentially compromised credentials.

The hackers’ identities remain unknown, but security experts say the incident illustrates an increasingly troubling risk as AI coding tools become embedded in developers’ workflows.

“The scenario of Claude sending out poisoned agents everywhere makes me even more worried than I already was,” says Eerke Boiten, a professor of cybersecurity at De Montfort University in England.

Gwen van der Velden, a professor of education at the University of Warwick who’s working on a program to help rebuild Ukraine, says the choice of the Claude Code extension is particularly “interesting” given the potential for such tools to be exploited in hybrid warfare.

“We know from the Russian side, it is of great interest to them,” she says. “If you were to go for hybrid warfare, where you use this kind of technology, then actually getting 5,000 bits of malware reproducing itself through AI agents is a powerful thing.”

The broader concern isn’t simply that a malicious extension could compromise individual computers. It’s that the growing ecosystem of AI coding assistants and their associated tools is creating new pathways into sensitive systems.

“This is a classic example of how everyone has been focussing on LLMs attacking other systems, yet forgetting about the fact that LLMs and their associated tools are increasing the attack surface across some very sensitive IT estates,” says Alan Woodward, a professor of cybersecurity at the University of Surrey.

And even a relatively limited breach could carry outsized consequences when the targets are software developers with access to sensitive code and infrastructure.

“While 5,000 users might sound relatively small, these are developers who have access to highly sensitive systems and source code, so the potential impact will be far greater than the numbers suggest,” says Jake Moore, a threat adviser with the global cybersecurity firm ESET. “Software extensions have eased their way into many people’s workflows, but the concern is how easily trusted software extensions can become a vehicle for malicious code.”

items.title: [canada.ca] Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk completes first spacewalk, installs ISS solar array
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Canadian Space Agency astronaut Colonel Joshua Kutryk and NASA astronaut Anil Menon completed a 7-hour, 11-minute spacewalk outside the International Space Station on Oct. 29, installing the seventh of eight planned solar arrays. Kutryk became the fifth Canadian astronaut to walk in space. The arrays are part of an upgrade campaign begun in 2021 that is expected to raise the station’s power-generation capacity by up to 30 per cent. Astronaut Jenni Gibbons served as capsule communicator, and Canadarm2, the station’s robotic arm, supported the installation. Kutryk and Menon are scheduled to install the final array during another spacewalk on Nov. 5.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] The asteroid killed the dinosaurs. Why did crocodiles survive?
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Scientists may have solved a 66-million-year-old mystery: how crocodiles survived the asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs. A sweeping analysis of fossils and ancient climates suggests that their preference for warm environments placed them in tropical refuges that remained habitable even after the catastrophic impact.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] A computer scientist breaks through a limit that stood since 1996
items.content_html: A computer scientist has achieved a breakthrough in a nearly 25-year-old problem involving how computers calculate distances across enormous networks. The new algorithm delivers more reliable estimates for closely connected points without sacrificing speed, overcoming a longstanding limitation of earlier methods. Its secret lies in a smarter way of sampling network connections at multiple scales.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Hubble reveals a stunning twist in how the universe emerged from darkness
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

A surprising discovery by astronomers using the Hubble Space Telescope is challenging a leading explanation for how the early universe emerged from a dense fog of hydrogen roughly 13 billion years ago. Scientists once believed powerful winds from exploding stars helped radiation escape galaxies and clear that cosmic fog, but new observations reveal that these winds actually block radiation instead.
